old_entry.title: Famicom / NES
old_entry.subtitle: Nintendo's cartridge console and its later NES design
old_entry.summary: Nintendo's Family Computer brought arcade games to Japanese homes in 1983. Redesigned as the NES, the same platform introduced millions more players to Mario, Zelda and Metroid.
body: On July 15, 1983 Nintendo launched the Family Computer, or Famicom, in Japan. The console arrived with Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr. and Popeye, three conversions that made its promise immediately clear: bring part of the arcade experience to the home television. Its price, built-in controllers, interchangeable cartridges and later opening to outside publishers created an ecosystem that would expand rapidly. When the machine was redesigned for overseas markets as the Nintendo Entertainment System, that Japanese project became one of the central models for the modern console industry.

Nintendo chooses three games already familiar from arcades, making the console's promise immediately testable: recognizable characters and actions on the television at home. Each offers a different experience. Donkey Kong asks players to read platforms and obstacles; its sequel shifts the action to ropes and climbing; Popeye builds a collection challenge around Bluto's pursuit. The initial catalogue therefore demonstrates three ways to organize a game around a clearly readable screen. At home, another attempt no longer requires another coin, allowing familiarity with those routes to develop through repeated sessions.

The red-and-white Famicom uses a top-loading cartridge slot and two controllers wired directly to the console. Recesses along its sides hold the pads, giving the system the proportions of a compact household object. A directional pad and the A and B buttons provide a consistent layout that very different games can share. The controllers are also deliberately unequal: the second includes a microphone instead of the first pad's Start and Select buttons. The design separates the machine's functions from the features individual programs can use. Changing the cartridge offers a new experience without requiring players to relearn the object in their hands.

Early Famicom revisions also affect the parts players touch most often. The original square A and B buttons give way to more durable round ones. In Nintendo's conversations about the period, the developers recall that players pressed harder than their experience with Game & Watch had led them to expect. This is a practical problem: a control can look perfectly clear in a design and prove unreliable after thousands of presses. A console's success also depends on such corrections. Controller durability becomes part of the experience alongside the software, because an unresponsive button directly interrupts the connection between a gesture and its result.

Nintendo brought the Nintendo Entertainment System to North America in 1985. It followed the Japanese Family Computer, or Famicom, introduced in 1983, but presented that platform in a different physical form. The grey front-loading case, detachable controllers and long cartridges belong to the western NES story.

Its small controller concentrated play around a directional pad and two main action buttons. Across the growing library, those few inputs could mean running and jumping, exploring a maze or choosing when to fight. Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda and Metroid helped give Nintendo's characters and worlds a place in everyday home life.

The European rollout began in 1986, with national markets following different schedules. It is also the story of how the same games reached different households through different objects, packaging and local experiences.

Nintendo brings the NES to the New York test market at a time when many American retailers consider it risky to devote space to new consoles after the industry crash of the early 1980s. To enter stores, Nintendo of America therefore has to sell not only a machine, but a different idea of the product. The system is presented as family entertainment, with accessories, packaging, and language designed to distance it from the image of older home video games. The New York test thus becomes a commercial experiment as well as a technological one.

The NES derives from Japan's Family Computer, but the transition to North America is not a simple name change. The machine is redesigned with a gray shell, lines closer to living-room electronics, and front-loading cartridges. The vocabulary changes too: cartridges become Game Paks and the console is presented as an Entertainment System. This transformation shows how industrial design can intervene in the perception of a technology. Nintendo does not hide the product's video game origins, but tries to place it in a commercial environment suspicious of the category. The result is a machine that looks very different from the red-and-white Famicom while sharing its technical foundation. Form, packaging, and terminology become tools for negotiating the video game's return to the US market.

At the North American debut, R.O.B. and the Zapper play a role greater than the number of games actually built around them. R.O.B., the Robotic Operating Buddy, makes the NES resemble an interactive toy and introduces physical movement in front of the television; the Zapper instead connects on-screen action to an immediately recognizable object. Nintendo still remembers R.O.B. as an NES accessory released in 1985, while Shigeru Miyamoto has described the choice of the name Zapper as a broader and less literal term than gun. In the context of the launch, these objects also help present a machine unlike the consoles retailers already knew. The peripheral therefore becomes communication: even before expanding gameplay, it helps the public understand how to look at the system.

The NES controller brings to North America a grammar already developed with the Famicom: a directional pad, two action buttons, Start, and Select. The layout is simple, but that simplicity makes the relationship between input and response immediate. The player learns to run, jump, shoot, or change rhythm through a few clearly separated inputs. The rectangular shape may appear rigid compared with later gamepads, but it establishes a reference that many 8-bit and 16-bit systems will adopt or reinterpret. Its importance lies not in the number of buttons, but in the predictability of the gesture. Each game can assign different functions without forcing the audience to relearn the machine from scratch. The controller thus becomes a stable interface between a highly varied library and a generation of players entering the medium.

The New York test market does not depend on a single title. Nintendo brings a catalog with the NES designed to show very different uses of the machine: sports, Zapper shooting, games tied to R.O.B., and platformers. Duck Hunt, Gyromite, Excitebike, and Super Mario Bros. nonetheless convey the platform's message: the NES is not a device with a single function, but a system whose identity changes through its Game Paks.

Nintendo progressively extends the NES to other US markets and expands North American distribution in 1986, turning the system into a mass-market platform. Nintendo's corporate history explicitly links the NES to the revival of the North American video game industry after the 1983 crisis. Success does not depend on a single element: recognizable hardware, first-party software, agreements with outside publishers, distribution control, and a coherent visual identity work together. Many conventions of the modern console market, from the centrality of exclusives to the relationship between platform and catalog, also take particularly visible form here.

editorial_features.title: The cartridge gate
body: The 1992 appellate opinion in Atari Games v. Nintendo describes a brief exchange before an NES cartridge could run. A chip in the console checked a coded message from a chip in an authorised game. Without that message, the console would refuse the cartridge. The 10NES system therefore made a commercial distinction operate through hardware and software. A box could fit the slot without gaining access to the television. Compatibility involved permission as well as the physical shape of the object somebody had bought.

The same opinion records Atari's entry into Nintendo's licensing system in December 1987. Nintendo manufactured cartridges carrying Atari's games, then sold them back for Atari to market. The agreement limited new NES releases and restricted release on rival home systems for two years. Those terms connected a programmer's finished work to a manufacturing and distribution arrangement. The later litigation concerned how Atari obtained and used the lockout program. Its findings should not be expanded into a claim that every form of examining compatible software was forbidden.

Retail prices presented another boundary, distinct from permission to publish a cartridge. In a May 1991 speech, FTC chair Janet Steiger discussed a proposed Nintendo consent agreement addressing allegations of resale price fixing. The announced remedy required Nintendo to refrain from controlling the prices at which dealers advertised or sold its products. This was an account of a specific enforcement process, not an explanation of every game price. It shows how a console business also depended on the relationship between a manufacturer and the shops serving customers.

Steiger highlighted cooperation with state authorities as part of that process. Her speech reported that thirty-nine states had accepted matching prospective relief, seeking consistent rules across the country. Behind a familiar branded console stood several sets of relationships: access for publishers, stock supplied to retailers and the conditions under which dealers could compete. The speech and the later lockout opinion concern different disputes. Reading them together reveals distinct points where commercial policy shaped how games reached a home, without turning either proceeding into a universal account of Nintendo's business.

Compatibility involved permission as well as the physical shape of the object somebody had bought.

The same opinion records Atari's entry into Nintendo's licensing system in December 1987. Nintendo manufactured cartridges carrying Atari's games, then sold them back for Atari to market. The agreement limited new NES releases and restricted release on rival home systems for two years. Those terms connected a programmer's finished work to a manufacturing and distribution arrangement. The later litigation concerned how Atari obtained and used the lockout program. Its findings should not be expanded into a claim that every form of examining compatible software was forbidden.

Retail prices presented another boundary, distinct from permission to publish a cartridge. In a May 1991 speech, FTC chair Janet Steiger discussed a proposed Nintendo consent agreement addressing allegations of resale price fixing. The announced remedy required Nintendo to refrain from controlling the prices at which dealers advertised or sold its products. This was an account of a specific enforcement process, not an explanation of every game price. It shows how a console business also depended on the relationship between a manufacturer and the shops serving customers.

Steiger highlighted cooperation with state authorities as part of that process. Her speech reported that thirty-nine states had accepted matching prospective relief, seeking consistent rules across the country. Behind a familiar branded console stood several sets of relationships: access for publishers, stock supplied to retailers and the conditions under which dealers could compete. The speech and the later lockout opinion concern different disputes. Reading them together reveals distinct points where commercial policy shaped how games reached a home, without turning either proceeding into a universal account of Nintendo's business.

The terms of access
A different commercial boundary
Rules across a market

paragraph_edits.old_body: The red-and-white Famicom uses a top-loading cartridge slot and two controllers wired directly to the console. Recesses along its sides hold the pads, giving the system the proportions of a compact household object. A directional pad and the A and B buttons provide a consistent layout that very different games can share. The controllers are also deliberately unequal: the second includes a microphone instead of the first pad's Start and Select buttons. The design separates the machine's functions from the features individual programs can use. Changing the cartridge offers a new experience without requiring players to relearn the object in their hands.

paragraph_edits.old_body: October 18, 1985 is not yet a nationwide launch. Nintendo brings the NES to the New York test market at a time when many American retailers consider it risky to devote space to new consoles after the industry crash of the early 1980s. To enter stores, Nintendo of America therefore has to sell not only a machine, but a different idea of the product. The system is presented as family entertainment, with accessories, packaging, and language designed to distance it from the image of older home video games. The New York test thus becomes a commercial experiment as well as a technological one. The NES does not conquer North America in a single day: October 18 marks the documented beginning of an expansion that will continue in 1986.

paragraph_edits.old_body: The NES derives from Japan's Family Computer, but the transition to North America is not a simple name change. The machine is redesigned with a gray shell, lines closer to living-room electronics, and front-loading cartridges. The vocabulary changes too: cartridges become Game Paks and the console is presented as an Entertainment System. This transformation shows how industrial design can intervene in the perception of a technology. Nintendo does not hide the product's video game origins, but tries to place it in a commercial environment suspicious of the category. The result is a machine that looks very different from the red-and-white Famicom while sharing its technical foundation. Form, packaging, and terminology become tools for negotiating the video game's return to the US market.

paragraph_edits.old_body: At the North American debut, R.O.B. and the Zapper play a role greater than the number of games actually built around them. R.O.B., the Robotic Operating Buddy, makes the NES resemble an interactive toy and introduces physical movement in front of the television; the Zapper instead connects on-screen action to an immediately recognizable object. Nintendo still remembers R.O.B. as an NES accessory released in 1985, while Shigeru Miyamoto has described the choice of the name Zapper as a broader and less literal term than gun. In the context of the launch, these objects also help present a machine unlike the consoles retailers already knew. The peripheral therefore becomes communication: even before expanding gameplay, it helps the public understand how to look at the system.

paragraph_edits.old_body: The NES controller brings to North America a grammar already developed with the Famicom: a directional pad, two action buttons, Start, and Select. The layout is simple, but that simplicity makes the relationship between input and response immediate. The player learns to run, jump, shoot, or change rhythm through a few clearly separated inputs. The rectangular shape may appear rigid compared with later gamepads, but it establishes a reference that many 8-bit and 16-bit systems will adopt or reinterpret. Its importance lies not in the number of buttons, but in the predictability of the gesture. Each game can assign different functions without forcing the audience to relearn the machine from scratch. The controller thus becomes a stable interface between a highly varied library and a generation of players entering the medium.

paragraph_edits.old_body: The New York test market does not depend on a single title. Nintendo brings a catalog with the NES designed to show very different uses of the machine: sports, Zapper shooting, games tied to R.O.B., and platformers. Reconstructing the 1985 launch through documentary evidence, however, requires caution: even the exact availability of Super Mario Bros. on the date indicated by Nintendo is difficult to prove with a complete commercial record. For this reason, the value of the catalog is best understood as part of the test-market phase, not as a rigidly certified list for one particular morning. Duck Hunt, Gyromite, Excitebike, and Super Mario Bros. nonetheless convey the platform's message: the NES is not a device with a single function, but a system whose identity changes through its Game Paks.

paragraph_edits.old_body: The historical value of October 18 is measured above all by what happens afterward. Nintendo progressively extends the NES to other US markets and expands North American distribution in 1986, turning the system into a mass-market platform. Nintendo's corporate history explicitly links the NES to the revival of the North American video game industry after the 1983 crisis. Success does not depend on a single element: recognizable hardware, first-party software, agreements with outside publishers, distribution control, and a coherent visual identity work together. Many conventions of the modern console market, from the centrality of exclusives to the relationship between platform and catalog, also take particularly visible form here. The New York test then appears as a starting point, not an isolated event.

old_entry.summary: Sony's first PlayStation joined real-time polygons to the capacity of a CD, giving developers new choices about what a console game could contain.
body: Open the lid and the change is easy to recognise. A PlayStation game sits on a compact disc, an object already familiar from recorded music. Sony launched the console in Japan on 3 December 1994; North America and Europe followed in September 1995. The format helped make room for more recorded sound, imagery and video, alongside the worlds being drawn in real time.

That capacity was a practical decision for developers as well as a selling point for players. Sony's history of the machine emphasises that CDs could hold more data than cartridge alternatives and could be manufactured more quickly and affordably. Games with large amounts of art and music, including Final Fantasy VII, could be built around those possibilities.

The new space did not dictate a single style. A racing game could make a circuit from polygons; an adventure could combine pre-rendered scenes with moving characters; a dramatic sequence could use recorded video. Designers had to decide where each technique helped the experience. More capacity created choices rather than automatically creating a better game.

The objects around the console also tell the story. A memory card held progress that could leave the machine, and the same disc drive could play an audio CD. PlayStation connected gaming with a wider household culture of music, screens and collected media. Its significance lies in the range of experiences that teams built from that combination.

On September 9, 1995, Sony Computer Entertainment launched the original PlayStation in North America, nine months after its Japanese debut and twenty days before its European arrival. The date therefore does not mark the console's worldwide birth, but one of the decisive stages of its international expansion. PlayStation brings into the home a machine designed around real-time polygonal graphics and CD-ROM, while Sony builds a new ecosystem for development and distribution. Ridge Racer and Tekken immediately demonstrate the appeal of three-dimensional arcade games, but the transformation is broader: optical media, controller, Memory Card, audio and brand image define a different way of thinking about the console. Within a single generation, PlayStation would become a platform capable of surpassing one hundred million units.

The history of PlayStation begins before the 1994 console. Sony had worked with Nintendo on a CD-ROM-based system for the Super Famicom, but the collaboration did not produce the intended product. Ken Kutaragi continued to support the idea of a Sony machine as the project shifted toward an independent platform designed for three-dimensional graphics. Sony's historical account shows how far this choice was from inevitable: there were doubts inside the company about entering video games at all. The first PlayStation therefore also tells a story of organizational change. It was born not only from a processor or optical medium, but from the decision to build a new format, a network of developers and an identity separate from Sony's already established electronics businesses.

The CD-ROM is not simply a container with more capacity than a cartridge. For Sony it becomes part of a different production model: large amounts of data, rapid duplication and lower manufacturing costs let publishers imagine games with more audio, video and content without relying on very expensive media. Sony's corporate history also links the disc to more direct distribution to retailers, reducing some traditional stages of the Japanese market. These conditions do not determine creativity by themselves, but they change a project's risk and the speed at which it can be reprinted. Very different titles, from arcade games to narrative productions spread across multiple discs, would exploit this flexibility. Technology therefore becomes economics as well: what goes into the console influences what can reach store shelves.

The original PlayStation was designed at a moment when real-time 3D was transforming arcades and beginning to redefine expectations for home consoles. Its 32-bit R3000 processor and graphics hardware were designed to move hundreds of thousands of polygons per second under ideal conditions. More important than the number is what it makes practical: moving cameras, characters built as volumes, tracks opening into depth and environments that demand new methods of orientation. Ridge Racer and Tekken communicate this direction immediately because they bring home experiences associated with three-dimensional arcades. The console does not eliminate 2D, but it makes the polygon a central language of the generation. Developers and players have to learn together how to read and control space.

The original controller keeps the directional pad but breaks with the flat shape typical of many earlier machines. Two grips stabilize the hold, and the four face buttons use symbols instead of letters: triangle, circle, cross and square. Designer Teiyu Goto explained that those shapes were conceived as simple, immediately recognizable icons. The choice quickly becomes part of PlayStation's identity because the same symbolism appears in tutorials, menus and platform communication. In 1995 the controller does not yet have the analog sticks that would become standard a few years later; its historical interest lies precisely in that point of transition. It tries to make the digital tradition more ergonomic while the console opens the door to increasingly three-dimensional games, preparing a form that Sony would continue to modify without abandoning it.

On the original PlayStation, progress is not stored automatically inside the console. Many games entrust save data to a Memory Card inserted into one of the two front slots, physically separating the playthrough from the disc. It is a technical solution, but it also creates a social habit: the card can be taken to a friend's house, replaced when space runs out and associated with a personal collection of characters, seasons or campaigns. The object makes visible something that would later become almost invisible with internal storage and cloud saves. Console, game and save file are three separate elements the player must manage. This materiality also influences interfaces, which have to show blocks, files and copy operations. The memory of a story literally coincides with a small object that must not be lost.

The North American launch on September 9, 1995 follows the strong visibility PlayStation gained at E3 earlier that year. Sony presents a new machine, but also searches for a tone that can distinguish it from a market perceived mainly through already established brands. The library quickly contributes to that identity: arcade games such as Ridge Racer and Tekken coexist with WipEout, then Resident Evil, Tomb Raider, Final Fantasy VII, Gran Turismo and Metal Gear Solid. There is no single PlayStation genre; the common trait is the sense that the home audience is expanding. Music, fashion, digital cinema and club culture enter the platform's communication alongside technology. PlayStation becomes recognizable not because it imposes one style, but because it offers many new ways to imagine who a player can be.

editorial_features.title: A shape becomes familiar
editorial_features.summary: Design survives a change of machinery.
body: The original PlayStation placed a round disc lid inside a rectangular case. Sony's institutional history describes this simple arrangement as part of the machine's identity, alongside its technical capabilities. The circle gave the storage medium a visible place in the object. Opening that lid was also a small physical ritual before play. A console could introduce itself through an understandable shape, then ask the television to reveal the complicated moving spaces its electronics were capable of building from a game disc.

Teiyu Goto gave the controller shapes that could work as icons. Sony's account also draws attention to its grips, a departure from the flat controllers familiar at the time. The object presented two related invitations: somewhere to place the hands, and marks to learn through use. Those geometric signs could travel beyond a particular game's instructions. A player looking down at the controller encountered a small visual vocabulary that belonged to the platform, alongside the different rules each game asked them to remember.

In September 2024, Hideaki Nishino introduced anniversary products that carried the first PlayStation's colour treatment onto contemporary hardware. PS5 consoles and DualSense controllers became surfaces for a remembered appearance. The announcement explicitly connected them to the December 1994 beginning. This was a design history told through objects people could use: a newer machine could retain its own capabilities while borrowing a familiar visual setting. The relationship depended on recognition, allowing a colour scheme to connect products separated by three decades of technical change.

The anniversary console bundles also included a cable connector housing styled after the original PlayStation controller, with cable ties shaped like the platform's symbols. A detail usually noticed while connecting or tidying a machine became a collector's object. These accessories extended the visual connection beyond the console case itself. The announcement shows how an industrial identity can move between scales: from the main machine to something held in the fingers, then to a small mark repeated among the cables around it.

old_entry.title: Music that moves with Mario
old_entry.summary: How can a tune help a player read a moving game?
body: Koji Kondo describes the original Super Mario Bros. score as a set of practical responses to the screen. The open ground, underwater passages, underground rooms and castle needed different musical identities. Limited sound resources did not make these locations interchangeable. A player could hear a change in surroundings as well as see it. That is a useful starting point for listening: compare the pace and texture of two locations before trying to name a favourite tune. The score helps divide a continuous adventure into situations with different expectations.

In his 2023 Library of Congress interview, Kondo explains that the Ground Theme combines evenly divided melody and bass parts with a differently divided percussion rhythm. He recalls finding that relationship by trying an idea rather than following a fixed formula. The result can be approached as a small arrangement of moving parts. Listen first to the melody, then to the accompaniment, then to their overlap. The music has forward motion without requiring every sound to strike together. Its apparent simplicity contains several kinds of timing working at once.

The same interview places music beside the game's changing conditions. Kondo describes short sounds for failure and success, and music that accelerates when little time remains. These are different jobs from establishing the atmosphere of a location. One marks an outcome; another changes the urgency of an action still in progress. Heard this way, the score is also part of the information available to the player. A familiar melody can remain recognisable while its function changes, turning listening into another way of knowing what is happening on screen.

In 2023 the Ground Theme entered the United States National Recording Registry, the first game recording selected for that collection. The work being recognised dates to 1985, while the archival decision belongs to a much later moment. Keeping those dates separate matters. A game tune can be heard during repeated play, then in arrangements and other settings, and eventually studied as a recording in its own right. The registry does not replace the original game context. It gives listeners another route back to the relationship between a tune, a machine and an action.

His first work at Nintendo was the audio design for the 1984 arcade game Punch-Out!!. As the Famicom had become popular in Japan, Kondo was assigned to compose music for the console's subsequent games at Nintendo's new development division, Nintendo Entertainment Analysis and Development (EAD). His second work at Nintendo was an instruction manual on how to program Japanese popular music into the Famicom using the peripheral Family BASIC. To conclude his first year at Nintendo, he created some of the music of Devil World, alongside Akito Nakatsuka. In 1985, Nintendo started marketing the Famicom abroad as the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) to capitalize on the 1983 video game crash that had devastated Atari, Inc. and other companies. Super Mario Bros., released that year, was Kondo's first major score. The game's melodies were created with the intention that short segments of music could be endlessly repeated during the same gameplay without causing boredom. The main theme is iconic in popular culture and has been featured in more than 50 concerts, been a best-selling ringtone, and been remixed or sampled by various musicians.

Kondo's music for Super Mario Bros. was designed around the feeling of motion that mirrors the player's physical experience. This followed the philosophy of series creator and designer Shigeru Miyamoto, who demanded that audio for the game be made "with substance" and synchronized with elements of the game. As a result, Kondo based most of the score around genres that are primarily used for dancing, such as Latin music and the waltz.

In the first The Legend of Zelda, Kondo juxtaposes the game's overworld theme with the theme that plays in dungeons. Kondo remarked on the importance of projecting distinct characters through music, so that players know almost immediately where they are within the game. Kondo used this contrast in other games, such as Super Mario Bros.

Ocarina of Time places an instrument in Link's hands and its gestures on the controller. Remembering a short sequence lets us affect the world: music becomes an ability to use. Kondo's work meets the player's memory, inviting us to take part in the performance rather than simply listen.

Kondo returned to the Super Mario series to produce the scores to Super Mario Bros. 3 (1988) and the SNES launch title Super Mario World (1990). Koichi Sugiyama directed a jazz arrangement album of Super Mario World's music and oversaw its performance at the first Orchestral Game Musical Concert in 1991. After finishing the soundtrack to Super Mario World, Kondo was in charge of the sound programming for Pilotwings (1990), while also composing the "Helicopter Theme" for it, and created the sound effects for Star Fox (1993). In 1995, he composed for the sequel to Super Mario World, Yoshi's Island. Until the early 2000s, Kondo would usually write all compositions by himself on a project, with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's being the last one Kondo worked on alone. Since then, he has been collaborating with other staff members at Nintendo, advising and supervising music created by others, as well as providing additional compositions for games, including Super Mario Galaxy, The Legend of Zelda: Spirit Tracks, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword and Super Mario 3D World. Kondo also served as the lead composer of Super Mario Maker and Super Mario Maker 2. He was a consultant for the score to The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023).

old_entry.title: Super Mario Bros.
old_entry.subtitle: A World That Teaches as You Move Through It
old_entry.summary: Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka's team built a readable landscape around the pleasure of a jump.
body: On September 13, 1985, Nintendo released Super Mario Bros. for the Family Computer in Japan. The game transforms experiments developed through Donkey Kong and Mario Bros. into a side-scrolling adventure built around running, jumping, transformation and discovery. Its importance does not depend only on commercial success or the birth of the Super Mario series. The opening minutes reveal a design method that explains rules through the placement of objects: the Goomba teaches danger, the block invites a jump, the mushroom is redirected toward Mario by a pipe, and the level guides the player without a separate tutorial. Even the protagonist's appearance emerges from concrete limits of readability. Super Mario Bros. turns technical constraint into part of a language that millions of people would learn by playing.

Nintendo recounts that World 1-1 was defined toward the end of development and continued to be adjusted until the final moments. The reason is visible in its precision. The first Goomba forces the player to discover jumping; the blocks overhead invite experimentation; the mushroom emerging from a block moves to the right and is sent back by the first pipe, increasing the chance that a beginner will collect it. Each element prepares the next and also accounts for plausible mistakes. The level does not assume that the player has read the manual, but it does not sacrifice future complexity. It teaches through immediate, repeatable consequences. This method makes instruction part of the pleasure: understanding a rule coincides with the moment when the player finally manages to use it.

Early Mario is born inside a grid of only 16 by 16 pixels. Shigeru Miyamoto has explained that the hat, moustache and overalls solve concrete problems: hair would be difficult to animate, the face has very little space, and arms the same color as the torso would make running harder to read. White gloves also help distinguish the movement of the hands. These solutions show how visual identity can emerge from functional necessity. Super Mario Bros. inherits an already recognizable character and places him at the center of a game in which body position has to be read in a fraction of a second. The silhouette is therefore not only a brand. It is an interface device: it communicates direction, jumping and transformation while the screen continues to scroll.

The Super Mushroom makes the character's growth visible: Mario increases in size, survives one hit and can interact differently with certain blocks. But the more refined part is how the game teaches that the object is desirable. Miyamoto recalled that the mushroom could be mistaken for an enemy with a similar shape. To solve the problem, the team made it move toward the player and designed the beginning of World 1-1 so that, after bouncing off the pipe, it would be difficult to avoid by accident. The explanation therefore happens through trajectory and space rather than a text window. The power-up becomes a small mechanical story: first it surprises, then it changes the body, and finally it lets the player understand in retrospect why it was worth collecting.

Super Mario Bros. has only a few fundamental actions, but it does not treat them as binary switches. Running, acceleration and the duration of a button press alter the trajectory, so the player learns to feel distance before expressing it in numbers. A wide pit is not read only with the eyes: it is compared with the available space for building speed and with the expected landing position. This continuity between input and movement allows levels to recombine the same elements without exhausting them quickly. A block, platform or enemy changes meaning depending on the speed at which Mario reaches it. Difficulty can therefore increase without constantly introducing new buttons. The repertoire remains small while the required precision grows. Mastery comes from the player's body as much as from memory of the maps.

Green pipes come from an everyday image, but in Super Mario Bros. they acquire a double function. At first they are solid obstacles that alter the trajectory of Mario and other objects; later, some become entrances to underground rooms or shortcuts. The player learns that the same shape can contain different possibilities. This controlled ambiguity feeds curiosity: once a traversable pipe has been discovered, every new pipe deserves at least an attempt. Level design creates a vocabulary that first establishes a rule and then introduces recognizable exceptions. Bonus areas and Warp Zones reward those who explore an apparently linear game, suggesting that the screen contains more space than is immediately visible. The path to the right remains clear, but the desire to deviate grows within that very clarity.

Nintendo describes Super Mario Bros. as the starting point of the series and one of the titles that fueled the Famicom boom. Its legacy, however, is most visible in conventions that have stopped feeling like inventions: the suspended block that invites a jump, the power-up that changes the body, the level that teaches through the order of obstacles, the flagpole as a visible ending. Many later games have reused, complicated or rejected these solutions, but they continue to engage with a vocabulary popularized in 1985. The title's historical strength therefore lies in the relationship between accessibility and depth. A beginner can understand what to do by observing a few signals; an expert can refine rhythm, trajectories and routes for years. The same space supports immediate learning and prolonged mastery.

Graph-paper plans preserve the world before it starts moving. Ground, pipes and obstacles occupy positions that must become instructions for the program. They reveal a level as an editable composition of measurements and revisions. A drawing cannot establish whether a sequence works: it has to be played. Between the paper and the controller, the design finally meets the player's sense of time.

Koji Kondo recalled that an early piece inspired by the scenery's sky and greenery did not match Mario's rhythm. The task was more than describing a pleasant place: it had to accompany a body running and jumping. The music's character emerges from that relationship. Its melody is memorable partly because it seems to understand our hands, allowing action and listening to belong to the same experience.

editorial_features.title: Paper, playtests and Mario's team
editorial_features.summary: Mario's levels took shape through shared revisions.
body: Before a Mario level could be tested, somebody had to translate a drawing into data. Toshihiko Nakago recalled receiving graph paper from Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, entering their layouts, then burning a ROM for them to play. Changes returned the following morning. The daily cycle made revision a shared production task rather than a designer's private gesture. A block moved on paper meant another person's work before its new position could be judged with a controller in the player's hands.

The sky levels almost disappeared, Nakago remembered, partly because of memory limits. Tezuka proposed a beanstalk; Miyamoto made it emerge from a struck block. Reaching the clouds exposed another problem: players might fear jumping down. An unnamed younger colleague suggested a trail of coins that invited the descent. This small sequence resists a simple inventor story. One person defended the destination, another shaped the entrance, and another made the exit understandable. The finished route held their contributions together for the player.

Tezuka later described levels that rarely worked as intended on their first attempt. He imagined an enemy arriving at a particular moment, then watched people behave differently. Revision meant responding to those actions, including the tendency to make a course too difficult when its designer already knew every obstacle. His account places testing between an attractive drawing and a finished level. The audience did not merely confirm the team's intention; its unexpected movements supplied information that could change the arrangement itself.

Koji Kondo's contribution arrived after the movement had become clear enough for him to imagine its sound, Tezuka recalled. Before that, Tezuka supplied his own jumping noises while playing. The eventual overworld and underground themes changed how the unfinished game felt to him. That recollection is useful because it restores another working relationship behind Mario's apparent simplicity. The visual rhythm did not automatically contain its music. A composer had to interpret movement, while the designers discovered what that interpretation added to play.

old_entry.title: Fairchild Channel F Videocarts
old_entry.summary: The Fairchild Channel F is a home video game console released by Fairchild Camera and Instrument in November 1976.
body: The Fairchild Channel F is a home video game console released by Fairchild Camera and Instrument in November 1976. It has the distinction of being the first programmable ROM cartridge-based video game console, and the first console to use a microprocessor. It was launched as the Fairchild Video Entertainment System, or Fairchild VES for short, but when Atari released their Atari Video Computer System, Atari VCS, later Atari 2600 the next year, Fairchild renamed its machine.

Twenty-seven cartridges, termed 'Videocarts', were officially released to consumers during the ownership of Fairchild and Zircon, the first twenty-one of which were released by Fairchild. Several of these cartridges were capable of playing more than one game. The Videocarts were yellow and approximately the size and overall texture of an 8 track cartridge. They usually featured colorful label artwork. Industrial designer Nicholas F. Talesforce was responsible for the overall design of the cartridges, while early artwork was created by artist Tom Kamifuji. The console contained two built-in games, Tennis and Hockey, which were both advanced Pong clones. In Hockey the reflecting bar could be changed to diagonals by twisting the controller, and could move all over the playing field. Tennis was much like the original Pong. These games were reviewed by Video magazine in 1978 and Hockey received a score of 7 out of 10 while Tennis received a 6 out of 10.

A sales brochure from 1978 listed 'Keyboard Videocarts' for sale. The three shown were  K-1 Casino Poker, K-2 Space Odyssey, and K-3 Pro-Football. These were intended to use the Keyboard accessory. All further brochures, released after Zircon took over Fairchild, never listed this accessory nor anything called a Keyboard Videocart.

One additional cartridge was released numbered Videocart-51 and titled 'Demo 1'. This Videocart was shown in a single sales brochure released shortly after Zircon acquired the company. It was never listed for sale after this single brochure used for the winter of 1979.

old_entry.summary: Star Fire is a first-person arcade coin-operated space combat video game created by Technical Magic for Midway-Bally and licensed for manufacture to Exidy in December 1978.
body: Star Fire is a first-person arcade coin-operated space combat video game created by Technical Magic for Midway-Bally and licensed for manufacture to Exidy in December 1978. It was distributed in Japan by Taito and Esco Trading in 1979. Designed by Ted Michon and David Rolfe and inspired by the film Star Wars, the game is not based on a licensed property.

Star Fire was a major success for Exidy, and became the first arcade video game to use an enclosed sit-down cockpit cabinet, the first to allow a highest scoring player to enter their initials in a high score table, and one of the first to be built on a reprogrammable microprocessor based game system with full screen color graphics. It was followed by an updated version, Star Fire II, with fixes. It was then ported by Epyx to Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit computers in a bundle with Fire One, another Exidy game.

old_entry.title: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar
old_entry.summary: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, first released in 1985 for the Apple II, is the fourth in the series of Ultima role-playing video games.
body: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, first released in 1985 for the Apple II, is the fourth in the series of Ultima role-playing video games. It is the first in the "Age of Enlightenment" trilogy, shifting the series from the hack and slash, dungeon crawl gameplay of its "Age of Darkness" predecessors towards an ethically nuanced, story-driven approach. Ultima IV has a much larger game world than its predecessors, with an overworld map sixteen times the size of Ultima III and puzzle-filled dungeon rooms to explore. Ultima IV further advances the franchise with dialog improvements, new means of travel and exploration, and world interactivity.

In 1996 Computer Gaming World named Ultima IV as #2 on its Best Games of All Time list for IBM PC compatibles. Designer Richard Garriott considers this game to be among his favorites from the Ultima series.
Ultima IV was followed by the release of Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny in 1988.
